title: Electrification in landscaping: transition to silent tools is slow
subtitle: The migration to electric and quieter equipment is not happening at the pace everyone expected.
excerpt: Electrification in landscaping advances with the search for quieter equipment, but the pace of the transition divides expectations regarding the speed of change.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
The landscaping and green area maintenance sector is undergoing an electrification process. This shift involves replacing traditional tools with electricity-powered versions. One of the main attractions of this transition is noise reduction, as the new electric equipment is considerably quieter. However, the pace of this technological migration has sparked debates, as the speed of the transition is not happening as quickly as some would like.

The role of silence in green area maintenance

Landscaping involves the constant care of lawns, trees, shrubs, and gardens in urban, residential, and commercial areas. To perform these tasks, professionals and enthusiasts use a variety of cutting, pruning, and cleaning tools. Historically, the machinery used in this sector has relied on internal combustion engines. The introduction of electric alternatives represents a change in how the maintenance of these green areas is planned and executed, focusing on alternatives that generate less noise during daily operations.

The pursuit of quieter equipment is a central aspect of the debate regarding the maintenance of public and private spaces. In residential areas, excessive noise caused by gardening tools can be a source of discomfort for residents and interfere with local well-being. Electric equipment, operating with engines that produce less noise, emerges as a solution to minimize noise pollution in cities. Noise reduction not only benefits the neighborhood but also improves working conditions for machine operators.

Challenges in the pace of technology adoption

The transition from an established technology to a new alternative, such as the electrification of equipment fleets, is a complex process involving various practical factors. The complete replacement of machinery requires planning, cost evaluation, and operator adaptation to new battery technologies and recharging systems. This scenario helps explain why the shift to electric and quieter tools may seem slow to those advocating for an immediate replacement of older models. The balance between the expectation of rapid change and the practical reality of technological adoption continues to define the pace of this process in landscaping.

With information from BBC News.
